subtopic_detail: Acting on a single raised prostate specific antigen result in an asymptomatic man
stem:
You are the general practice registrar reviewing a 58 year old accountant who asked for a prostate check at his last visit after a colleague was diagnosed with prostate cancer. He has no urinary symptoms and no first degree relative with prostate cancer.

He has not cycled, ejaculated or had a urinary catheter in the week before the blood test, and he takes no finasteride or dutasteride. Digital rectal examination performed today finds a smooth, symmetrical gland without nodularity. A midstream urine was collected at the same visit as the blood test.

data_table.Examination: Smooth symmetrical prostate without nodules, abdomen soft, no bony tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Prostate specific antigen 5.2 mcg/L, midstream urine no growth and no pyuria, creatinine within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the prostate specific antigen within one to three months
options.rationale: Australian practice is to confirm an initial elevation with a second sample within one to three months before any referral, because biological variation, unrecognised prostatitis and recent instrumentation mean a substantial share of raised results settle on repeat (Source: Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines).
source_refs: Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines

options.text: Refer to urology now for transperineal prostate biopsy
options.rationale: Referral for tissue sampling follows a confirmed elevation, and proceeding on one unconfirmed result exposes a man to sepsis and haematuria for a value that may normalise (Source: Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines).
source_refs: Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines

options.text: Arrange multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging of the prostate
options.rationale: Multiparametric imaging is the right next test once the elevation is confirmed and the man has accepted a diagnostic pathway, but it sits after confirmation rather than replacing it (Source: Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines).
source_refs: Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines

options.text: Reassure him and repeat the blood test in two years
options.rationale: A two yearly interval applies to men whose result sits below the age related threshold, and applying it to a value of 5.2 mcg/L defers a genuinely abnormal result (Source: RACGP: Guidelines for preventive activities in general practice).
source_refs: RACGP: Guidelines for preventive activities in general practice

options.text: Prescribe four weeks of ciprofloxacin then repeat the blood test
options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics to lower the value are a recognised anti pattern that delays diagnosis, and the sterile urine without pyuria gives no support for treating prostatitis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Prostate specific antigen testing in Australia is an informed decision rather than a population screening program, offered every two years from age 50 to 69 to men who choose to test after a discussion of benefits and harms. Age related thresholds are used because the reference range rises with prostatic volume, and a result above the threshold triggers confirmation rather than immediate referral. Ejaculation, vigorous cycling, digital rectal examination, urinary infection and instrumentation all raise the value transiently, while five alpha reductase inhibitors halve it and require the result to be doubled for interpretation. Men with a first degree relative diagnosed young, or with a known pathogenic BRCA2 variant, start testing earlier and test more often. The harm the pathway is designed to avoid is overdiagnosis of indolent disease, which is why active surveillance features heavily once low risk cancer is found.
key_points: Confirm an initial raised result with a repeat sample in one to three months before referring.
Testing is offered two yearly from 50 to 69 years after an informed decision, not as universal screening.
Ejaculation, cycling, infection and instrumentation transiently raise the value.
Five alpha reductase inhibitors halve the measured value, so double it before comparing with the threshold.
Digital rectal examination is not used alone as a screening test in primary care.
explanation.pearls: A man taking finasteride or dutasteride for six months or more has a measured value about half his true value, so a reading of 2.5 mcg/L on treatment should be read as 5 mcg/L and acted on accordingly.

sources.label: Prostate Cancer Foundation of Australia and Cancer Council Australia: PSA testing guidelines
RACGP: Guidelines for preventive activities in general practice

subtopic_detail: Reversing warfarin in the presence of clinically significant bleeding
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the emergency department for a 78 year old woman who has passed three black tarry stools since last night and feels faint on standing. She takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation and finished a course of trimethoprim for a urinary infection four days ago.

She is alert and orientated. There is no external bleeding and no neurological deficit. Two large bore cannulas are in place, group and hold has been sent and the gastroenterology team has been contacted about endoscopy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 92/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: International normalised ratio 6.2 (0.8-1.2), haemoglobin 76 g/L (115-165), platelets 214 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 104 micromol/L (45-90)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate reversal strategy?

options.text: Withhold warfarin and recheck the international normalised ratio in six hours
options.rationale: Simple omission is the strategy for a raised value without bleeding, and it leaves this woman anticoagulated for another day while she continues to bleed (Source: Australasian Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis: Warfarin reversal consensus guidelines).
source_refs: Australasian Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis: Warfarin reversal consensus guidelines

options.text: Give intravenous vitamin K with prothrombin complex concentrate
options.rationale: Clinically significant bleeding on warfarin calls for immediate factor replacement, which restores the vitamin K dependent factors within minutes, together with intravenous vitamin K to sustain the correction once the concentrate is cleared (Source: Australasian Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis: Warfarin reversal consensus guidelines).
source_refs: Australasian Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis: Warfarin reversal consensus guidelines

options.text: Give intravenous vitamin K alone and repeat it after twelve hours
options.rationale: Vitamin K takes six to eight hours to begin correcting and up to a day for full effect because new factor synthesis is required, so it cannot be the sole agent when bleeding is active (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Transfuse four units of fresh frozen plasma without other agents
options.rationale: Plasma is the near pair and remains the fallback where concentrate is unavailable, but it corrects incompletely and delivers a large volume load to an older woman, so it is second choice (Source: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines).
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines

options.text: Give intravenous tranexamic acid and transfuse two units of red cells
options.rationale: Red cells and antifibrinolytics address the consequences of blood loss rather than the coagulopathy driving it, and neither lowers the international normalised ratio (Source: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines).
source_refs: National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines

explanation.summary: Warfarin reversal is graded by whether bleeding is present and how severe it is, not by the numerical value alone. With no bleeding and a value under 10, omitting doses with or without low dose oral vitamin K is enough; with no bleeding and a value of 10 or above, oral vitamin K is added; with clinically significant bleeding, factor replacement is given regardless of the number. Trimethoprim, metronidazole, amiodarone, fluconazole and the macrolides are common Australian precipitants of a sudden rise because they inhibit warfarin metabolism or displace it. The dose of intravenous vitamin K used in bleeding is deliberately high because the aim is durable correction rather than preserving future warfarin sensitivity. Restarting anticoagulation after the bleeding source is controlled is a separate decision that weighs stroke risk against rebleeding, and in atrial fibrillation it is usually resumed within days.
key_points: Clinically significant bleeding on warfarin means factor concentrate plus intravenous vitamin K, whatever the number.
Vitamin K alone takes six to twenty four hours because it requires new factor synthesis.
Fresh frozen plasma is the fallback only when concentrate is unavailable.
Trimethoprim and other enzyme inhibitors are frequent precipitants of a sudden rise.
A raised value without bleeding is managed by omission with or without oral vitamin K.
explanation.pearls: Prothrombinex-VF is dosed at 25 to 50 units per kilogram by indication and corrects the international normalised ratio within about fifteen minutes, but its factor half life is shorter than warfarin's, so omitting the concurrent vitamin K produces rebound coagulopathy overnight.

sources.label: Australasian Society of Thrombosis and Haemostasis: Warfarin reversal consensus guidelines
National Blood Authority: Patient Blood Management Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Separating an inflammatory arthritis with dactylitis from a post infective arthritis
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the rheumatology clinic seeing a 38 year old plumber with eight weeks of joint pain. Six weeks before the joints began he had four days of bloody diarrhoea after a work barbecue, which settled without treatment.

The right second toe and the left third finger are swollen along their whole length rather than at the joint lines, and the right knee and left ankle are swollen and warm. The distal interphalangeal joints of both hands are tender. Several fingernails show pinpoint depressions in the nail plate and there is thickened scaling behind both ears and at the umbilicus. Eye examination is normal and there is no urethral discharge.

data_table.Examination: Sausage swelling of the right second toe and left third finger, warm effusions in the right knee and left ankle, pitting of four fingernails
data_table.Investigations: C reactive protein 38 mg/L (less than 5), rheumatoid factor not detected, anti cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody not detected, serum urate 0.34 mmol/L (0.20-0.42), stool culture no growth

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Reactive arthritis triggered by the recent enteric infection
options.rationale: The enteric illness fits the timing, but reactive arthritis does not produce nail pitting or scaly plaques, and it usually brings conjunctivitis or urethritis, both absent here (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).

options.text: Seronegative rheumatoid arthritis with early joint swelling
options.rationale: Rheumatoid disease is symmetrical, spares the distal interphalangeal joints and does not cause whole digit swelling, so the distribution here argues against it despite the negative serology (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Psoriatic arthritis).

options.text: Psoriatic arthritis with dactylitis and nail involvement
options.rationale: Whole digit swelling from combined tenosynovitis and synovitis, distal interphalangeal involvement, nail pitting and hidden scalp and umbilical plaques together make this the diagnosis even when the patient has never reported a skin condition (Source: Australian Rheumatology Association: Psoriatic arthritis).

options.text: Polyarticular gout with a chronic tophaceous component
options.rationale: Gout can involve the toe and knee together, but a serum urate of 0.34 mmol/L between attacks and the absence of tophi make crystal disease an unlikely explanation for eight weeks of swelling (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).

options.text: Disseminated gonococcal infection with tenosynovitis
options.rationale: Gonococcal disease produces migratory tenosynovitis with pustular skin lesions over days to a fortnight, not eight weeks of persistent swelling with nail changes (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

explanation.summary: Psoriatic arthritis is under recognised because up to a sixth of patients present with joints before skin, and the skin that is present hides in the scalp, natal cleft, umbilicus and nails. Its five recognised patterns are asymmetric oligoarthritis, distal interphalangeal predominant disease, symmetric polyarthritis resembling rheumatoid disease, spondylitis, and arthritis mutilans. Dactylitis reflects inflammation of the flexor tendon sheath as well as the joint, which is why the whole digit swells rather than the joint line alone. Diagnosis is clinical and supported by the classification criteria, since no serological test confirms it and inflammatory markers are normal in a third of patients. Early treatment matters because erosive damage accrues within the first two years, and methotrexate or a targeted biologic is started rather than waiting for radiographic change.
key_points: Examine the scalp, umbilicus, natal cleft and nails when an inflammatory arthritis has no obvious skin disease.
Dactylitis is whole digit swelling from tenosynovitis plus synovitis and is highly suggestive.
Distal interphalangeal involvement separates this from rheumatoid arthritis, which spares those joints.
Normal inflammatory markers occur in about a third of patients and do not exclude the diagnosis.
Reactive arthritis needs a mucocutaneous clue such as conjunctivitis, urethritis or keratoderma.
explanation.pearls: Nail pitting of more than twenty pits across the fingernails carries a strong association with distal interphalangeal joint disease, because the nail matrix and the extensor enthesis of that joint share a continuous connective tissue attachment.

subtopic_detail: Choosing the screening test for suspected growth hormone excess
stem:
You are the general medical registrar assessing a 46 year old man referred with hypertension that has needed three agents over two years. His wife brought old photographs to the consultation and you can see that his jaw and brow have coarsened.

He volunteers that his wedding ring had to be cut off last year and that he has gone up three shoe sizes since his thirties. He sweats through two shirts a day and snores heavily with witnessed pauses. On examination there is spacing between the lower incisors and the tongue is enlarged. Fasting glucose is 7.4 mmol/L and thyroid function is within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 158/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 7.4 mmol/L (3.0-5.4), thyroid stimulating hormone within normal limits, calcium corrected 2.44 mmol/L (2.10-2.60)

lead_in: Which initial investigation would best establish the diagnosis?

options.text: Random serum growth hormone measured on a single morning sample
options.rationale: Growth hormone is secreted in pulses with troughs that reach the undetectable range in healthy people, so a single value neither confirms nor excludes excess (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Oral glucose tolerance test with paired growth hormone sampling
options.rationale: Failure of growth hormone to suppress after a glucose load is the near pair and remains the confirmatory test, but it is used to resolve an equivocal or discordant screening result rather than as the first step (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Acromegaly).
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Acromegaly

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary fossa with contrast
options.rationale: Imaging localises a lesion once biochemical excess is proven, and performing it first risks acting on an incidental pituitary lesion found in about a tenth of adults (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Serum insulin like growth factor 1 interpreted against age matched values
options.rationale: This peptide has a half life of many hours and reflects integrated growth hormone secretion across the day, so a single sample compared with an age matched range is the recommended screening test (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Acromegaly).
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Acromegaly

options.text: Overnight dexamethasone suppression test with morning serum cortisol
options.rationale: Cortisol excess would explain hypertension and glucose intolerance but not acral enlargement, interdental spacing or macroglossia, and there are no striae or proximal weakness (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: Growth hormone excess in adults advances slowly enough that neither the patient nor the family notices, so the diagnosis is typically made about a decade after onset and is often prompted by comparing old photographs. Hypertension, type 2 diabetes, obstructive sleep apnoea, carpal tunnel syndrome and arthropathy are the systemic consequences that bring the patient to medical attention. Screening is biochemical and localisation follows, because pituitary incidentalomas are common enough that imaging first generates confusion. Most cases arise from a somatotroph macroadenoma, so visual fields and anterior pituitary function are assessed once the diagnosis is biochemically established. Untreated disease roughly doubles mortality, driven by cardiovascular disease, and there is an increased incidence of colorectal neoplasia that shapes surveillance.
key_points: Insulin like growth factor 1 against an age matched range is the screening test.
Random growth hormone is uninterpretable because secretion is pulsatile.
Failure to suppress growth hormone after an oral glucose load is confirmatory when screening is equivocal.
Image the pituitary only after biochemical confirmation, given the frequency of incidentalomas.
Hypertension, diabetes, sleep apnoea and arthropathy drive the excess mortality.
explanation.pearls: Old photographs spanning ten to fifteen years are a genuine diagnostic instrument here: soft tissue change of this speed is invisible to daily observers, and the photographic comparison often precedes the biochemistry by a single consultation.

sources.label: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Acromegaly

subtopic_detail: Next test after raised ferritin with a high transferrin saturation in a middle aged man
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a 44 year old man in clinic with eighteen months of tiredness and aching in the knuckles of both hands. He tells you his older brother was told he had too much iron and now gives blood regularly at the hospital.

He drinks four standard drinks a week and takes no supplements, no iron tablets and no over the counter tonics. The second and third metacarpophalangeal joints are tender with bony swelling. There is no palpable liver edge, no spider naevi and no ascites. Hepatitis B and C serology is negative and his C reactive protein is 3 mg/L.

data_table.Examination: Tender bony swelling of the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints, no hepatomegaly, no stigmata of chronic liver disease
data_table.Investigations: Ferritin 1480 mcg/L (30-300), transferrin saturation 71 per cent (16-45), alanine aminotransferase 68 U/L (less than 41), C reactive protein 3 mg/L (less than 5), full blood count within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Percutaneous liver biopsy to quantify the hepatic iron concentration
options.rationale: Biopsy has been displaced from the diagnostic pathway by genetic testing and now serves mainly to stage fibrosis when ferritin exceeds 1000 mcg/L, so it follows rather than precedes the genotype (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Haemochromatosis).

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the liver to estimate iron concentration
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance quantification is a non invasive alternative for measuring hepatic iron and monitoring response, but it does not identify the inherited defect that determines family testing (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Haemochromatosis).

options.text: Repeat fasting iron studies with inflammatory markers in three months
options.rationale: Repeating is the right move when ferritin is raised with a normal saturation, since ferritin behaves as an acute phase reactant, but a saturation of 71 per cent with a C reactive protein of 3 mg/L already excludes that explanation (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Haemochromatosis).

options.text: Commence weekly venesection and reassess the ferritin after ten weeks
options.rationale: Venesection is the correct treatment but starting it before genotyping removes the chance to confirm the diagnosis and denies his siblings and children a clear basis for cascade testing (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Haemochromatosis).

options.text: HFE genotyping for the C282Y and H63D variants on peripheral blood
options.rationale: A transferrin saturation above 45 per cent with a raised ferritin in a man with a suggestive family history is the trigger for genotyping, and confirming C282Y homozygosity establishes the diagnosis and enables cascade screening of relatives (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Haemochromatosis).

explanation.summary: Hereditary haemochromatosis is the commonest inherited disorder in Australians of northern European ancestry, and the great majority of clinically affected people are homozygous for the C282Y variant of the HFE gene. Transferrin saturation rises before ferritin and is the more specific screening measure, since ferritin alone rises with alcohol, obesity, metabolic dysfunction associated fatty liver and any inflammatory state. The second and third metacarpophalangeal joints are the classical arthropathy and often the earliest symptom, preceding diabetes, cardiomyopathy, hypogonadism and cirrhosis. Treatment is weekly venesection to a ferritin target of 50 to 100 mcg/L followed by lifelong maintenance every three to four months. Confirming the genotype matters beyond the individual, because first degree relatives can then be offered testing before organ damage occurs.
key_points: Transferrin saturation above 45 per cent with raised ferritin triggers HFE genotyping.
Ferritin alone is an acute phase reactant and rises with alcohol, obesity and inflammation.
Second and third metacarpophalangeal arthropathy is often the earliest clinical feature.
Genotype first so that cascade testing of first degree relatives has a defined target.
Liver biopsy now stages fibrosis in high ferritin disease rather than making the diagnosis.
explanation.pearls: Ferritin above 1000 mcg/L with a raised alanine aminotransferase identifies the subgroup at real risk of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma, and this is the threshold at which fibrosis staging is added rather than proceeding straight to venesection alone.
